planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in early spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil, ideally in groups where the chalky-white, black-fissured bark reads well against a dark backdrop; European white birch struggles in prolonged summer heat, so it is best suited to the cooler half of its range.

directions: Plant in cool, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; European white birch is a fast-growing pioneer tree from Europe and northern Asia, prized for its slender white trunks that develop deep black diamond-shaped fissures with age and for its fine, fluttering foliage carried on gracefully drooping branchlets. Grow it as a specimen or in a clustered grove where the bark and airy silhouette can be appreciated through the dormant season, and keep the shallow root zone mulched and consistently moist, since heat- or drought-stressed trees are vulnerable to bronze birch borer. Fall color is a clear butter yellow. It performs best in northern and cool-summer gardens and declines in the humid heat of the Southeast.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America

common_name: Young's Weeping Birch (Weeping European White Birch)

planting.note: Plant grafted, container-grown trees in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Youngii is typically top-grafted at 5-6 feet, so the cascading branches form a distinctive umbrella-shaped mound from a single trunk height rather than a tall tree.

directions: Young's Weeping Birch is a compact, strongly pendulous cultivar of European white birch, its slender branches cascading nearly to the ground from a graft point to form a broad, mounded, umbrella-like crown far shorter and wider than the species. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; the striking white, black-fissured bark and weeping silhouette make it a classic focal point for a lawn or courtyard where its full form can be seen from a distance. Keep roots cool and mulched and avoid hot, dry, compacted sites, since stressed trees are prone to bronze birch borer and leaf miner. Prune only to remove crossing or rubbing branches, working from the graft union outward to preserve the natural cascading form.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in early spring or fall in cool, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Cutleaf Weeping Birch grows more upright than Young's Weeping Birch, with weeping habit concentrated in the branchlets rather than the whole crown.

directions: Cutleaf Weeping Birch, long grown in Scandinavia and sometimes sold as Swedish birch, combines the white, black-fissured bark of European white birch with finely dissected, deeply cut, fern-like leaves that give the canopy an unusually lacy, delicate texture. It grows taller and more upright than Young's Weeping Birch, with pendulous branchlets rather than a fully cascading crown, making it more useful as a genuine shade tree with ornamental drape at the branch tips. Plant in cool, moist, well-drained soil in full sun and keep the shallow roots mulched, since heat- or drought-stressed trees are susceptible to bronze birch borer. Fall color is a soft yellow, and the open canopy allows dappled light through to underplantings.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees, often as multi-stem clumps, in early spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; site where the brilliant white trunks are visible against a dark backdrop or winter sky.

directions: Himalayan birch is native to high-elevation forests of the western Himalayas, where it grows at some of the highest tree-line elevations of any birch. It is grown for the whitest bark of any commonly cultivated birch, exfoliating in thin, papery curls to reveal a smooth, brilliant chalk-white trunk that intensifies with age and provides outstanding winter interest, especially in multi-stem clump form. Give it cool, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun and mulch the shallow root zone, since drought- or heat-stressed trees remain vulnerable to bronze birch borer. Fall color is a clear gold, and the tree is most dramatic planted in a grove or against evergreens where the white trunks stand out through the dormant season.

common_name: Columnaris European Hornbeam (Dense Narrow Columnar Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun to partial shade; Columnaris is slower-growing and denser than Fastigiata and holds a truly narrow, symmetrical form for life rather than widening with age.

directions: Columnaris is an older, denser European hornbeam selection distinguished from the more commonly planted Fastigiata by its slower growth and truly narrow, egg-shaped to columnar crown, which stays tight and symmetrical at maturity instead of broadening into a wide oval. Its fine, densely twiggy branching and winter marcescence (retained tan leaves) give it strong structural presence and screening value even in the dormant season. Grow in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates clay soils, urban pollution, and root-zone compaction as well as the species. Because it keeps its narrow silhouette for decades, it is especially useful for tight side yards, formal allees, and street strips where long-term predictability matters more than fast establishment.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun to partial shade; stake the leader while young to establish head height, since the weeping habit otherwise keeps growth low and spreading.

directions: Weeping European Hornbeam is a rare, slow-growing selection in which the branches arch and cascade downward from the main framework, building over time into a broad, mounded, umbrella-shaped canopy that is usually wider than it is tall. Like the species it retains dried tan leaves through winter, giving the weeping silhouette structure and texture even in the dormant season, and it shares the same tolerance for clay soil and urban conditions. Grow in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun to partial shade, and stake young trees to build head height before the pendulous habit takes over. It makes a distinctive specimen for a lawn focal point where its unusual cascading form has room to develop without crowding.

planting.note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, average to lean, loamy or rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean hornbeam tolerates drier, thinner soils than European or American hornbeam.

directions: Korean hornbeam is the smallest of the commonly cultivated hornbeams, native to Korea, Japan, and eastern China, where it grows on dry, rocky slopes as a shrubby small tree. Its fine-textured, small, deeply veined leaves and dense, twiggy, often multi-stemmed branching give it a refined, tidy appearance well suited to small gardens, and it is a favored species for bonsai for the same reasons. Grow in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun to partial shade; it is more drought- and heat-tolerant than European hornbeam once established. Fall color is an attractive orange to red, and the smooth gray bark develops shallow furrows with age, adding winter interest to this underused small ornamental tree.

planting.note: Plant seeds in fall for natural stratification or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, rocky or alkaline soil in full sun; Oriental hornbeam tolerates dry, thin, limestone soils far better than European hornbeam.

directions: Oriental hornbeam is a small, shrubby tree native to dry rocky hillsides and open woodland of southeastern Europe and Asia Minor, closely related to European hornbeam but noticeably smaller in every dimension, with tiny, finely toothed leaves and a dense, twiggy, rounded habit. Its compact size and remarkable drought and heat tolerance once established make it valuable where larger hornbeams would be too big or too demanding of moisture, including dry hedges, screens, and clipped topiary forms. Grow in well-drained, lean to average soil, including rocky or alkaline sites, in full sun; established plants need little supplemental water. Fall color is a modest yellow, and the fine-textured foliage and tolerance of shearing make it an excellent, underused alternative to boxwood or privet for a dense, drought-tolerant hedge.
